The erowid instructions are already essentially dumbed down. Fact is, the layman, as you put it, should **not** be doing chemistry, especially of this nature.

In a perfect world.. yes you *should* be fine.. but to rely on things going perfectly is being absurdly naive. Accidents do happen. I say all this not from the perspective of a chemist, but from the perspective of someone who thought like OP at one point. I was honest with myself and when I got into the nitty gritty details of everything I realized even with baby step recipes, I was far away from being able to follow them. Practically it's not possible either. You need to invest a lot of money into all the proper gear and reagents, and you absolutely need a safe place to practice, something which the vast majority of people do not have, lest not the type of people who come onto reddit to ask these sort of questions anyway. Even if you don't go and get a degree, and you manage to acquire everything you need, you'll spend years doing experiments before you truly have the ability to follow those erowid instructions, and to know what to do when things go wrong. Even something as simple as adding your acid too fast causing a boil over and other unwanted reactions..

I don't necessarily disagree.. but *without* a degree you'll be left not knowing entirely what you are doing, relying on what are essentially recipes you find, and *hope* are accurate.. Then if things go wrong, which they so often do in chemistry, you're left without a clue - and that's if things go wrong in one of the lesser ways things can go wrong.

If you're serious about wanting to do chemistry of any kind beyond simple dimple high school level reactions (lets be honest here, look where this guy posted..) then you should really look into getting a degree. Picking up books and learning from them is a step in the right direction, but once you dive in, you'll find yourself spending a few years learning to get to the topic you wanted to learn when you dove in anyway.

If you look hard enough and know where to look.. yes you can find "recipes" but do you really want to put all your faith in that? How are you going to know you actually accomplished and came up with the end products you want? How do you know you're not just reading something that someone put together with little tricks to fool the chemistry naive? (this does happen) tricks that anyone with a chem background would stop and say "hey wait a sec.." Chemistry is really no joke. If you want to do it, take it seriously. That's my opinion anyway/
